unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume Hastings was inevitable — that Norman cavalry and archers were always going to overwhelm a 'primitive' Anglo-Saxon shield wall. In reality the housecarls were elite, the shield wall held until late afternoon, and historians stress how close-run the battle was; Harold's death (whatever the cause) was the decisive accident.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE History 8145 examiner reports flag thin causation on Hastings; Marc Morris, The Norman Conquest (2012); English Heritage 'What Happened at the Battle of Hastings'

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat castles as purely defensive. They were instruments of conquest first — projection of lordly power, control of road junctions and river crossings, intimidation of nearby populations — and only secondarily defensive structures.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: English Heritage 'Norman Castles' overview; History Today articles on motte-and-bailey colonisation

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students think Domesday was a legal land registry to settle property disputes. Its primary purposes were fiscal (raising geld and assessing tax capacity) and political (recording the new Norman tenurial structure and tenants-in-chief), not adjudicative.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: The National Archives 'Spotlight On: Domesday Book'; History Today 'Domesday in the Middle Ages: Usage and Abusage'

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students treat 'the Normans' as one homogeneous group. William's invasion army was a coalition — Normans, Bretons, Flemings, French — and his post-conquest aristocracy reflected that mix; calling everyone 'Norman' obscures the patronage politics.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: Marc Morris, The Norman Conquest; Hugh Thomas, The English and the Normans (2003)

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students either downplay it ('just a punitive raid') or treat Orderic Vitalis's claim of 100,000 dead as straight fact. Modern historians sit between: scale of destruction was real and unprecedented, but contemporary chroniclers writing decades later inflated numbers, and Domesday's 'waste' entries are now read with caution.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: History Today 'The Harrying of the North'; Hugh Thomas's The English and the Normans

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students think 'feudalism' was a system William sat down and designed. It was a working pattern of landholding-for-service that evolved, with the king at the top, tenants-in-chief, sub-tenants and peasants — and historians now debate whether 'feudalism' as a single system even existed.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: AQA examiner commentary on weak feudal-system answers; Susan Reynolds, Fiefs and Vassals (1994)

unit_specific_misconceptions.misconception: Students assume the Anglo-Saxon Church was 'corrupt' and Lanfranc 'cleaned it up'. The pre-1066 Church had its own learning and reform impulses; Lanfranc's changes were as much about Norman political control (replacing bishops, building cathedrals, reorienting monasticism) as about doctrinal cleanup.
unit_specific_misconceptions.source: English Heritage 'Beyond 1066: the real story of the Norman Conquest'; History Today on Lanfranc and Anselm

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 16-mark historic environment essay, top-band answers explicitly tie features of Pevensey Castle (Roman walls, peninsula site, inner bailey, the 1088 siege) to wider depth-study themes — conquest, control, William II's reign — rather than describing the site in isolation.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B; Oxford University Press blog 'How to tackle the Historic Environment question in AQA GCSE History'

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On the 8-mark 'Explain the Importance' question, students must choose two factors and weigh them — not just describe two things. Importance means consequences for the period, not just 'it happened'.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: Save My Exams summary of AQA GCSE History 8145 Q2 marking guidance (signposting only — drawn from publicly released mark schemes)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: On 4-mark 'Describe Two Features' questions, examiners reward a precise feature plus a developed sentence of detail per feature — no need for analysis, but vague labels ('the feudal system was important') score nothing.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA GCSE History 8145 Paper 2B/A mark schemes (June 2018 onwards)

examiner_signals_unit_specific.signal: Historic environment essays consistently reward use of named features of the specific site. For Pevensey 2026, examiners will expect candidates to deploy 'Roman walls', 'inner bailey', 'Robert of Mortain', '1088 siege' as concrete anchors, not generic 'castle' language.
examiner_signals_unit_specific.source: AQA released 2019 mark scheme for Pevensey Castle paper (the previous time Pevensey was the specified site)

historiography.summary: Hugh Thomas (The English and the Normans, 2003) argues for substantial Anglo-Saxon continuity — language, law, local administration, peasant life — beneath a thin Norman ruling crust. Marc Morris (The Norman Conquest, 2012) emphasises rupture — wholesale dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy, transformation of Church personnel, the violence of the Harrying.
historiography.source: Public-facing summaries on History Today and English Heritage 'Beyond 1066'

historiography.summary: Older scholarship treated Orderic Vitalis's '100,000 dead' as broadly credible; recent work (drawing on archaeology and re-reading Domesday's 'waste' entries) sits between catastrophic-genocide claims and a measured-destruction reading. Either way, the political effect — terror that ended large-scale northern revolt — is undisputed.
historiography.source: History Today 'The Harrying of the North'

historiography.summary: Susan Reynolds (Fiefs and Vassals, 1994) argued the 'feudal system' is a 19th-century historians' construct that flattens varied real practices. AQA still teaches feudalism as a working model because students need a framework — but examiners reward students who can describe the real working relationships (military service, land grants, sub-infeudation) rather than chant a textbook hierarchy.
historiography.source: Public scholarship referenced in Oxford and Hodder GCSE textbooks

pedagogy_notes: Order matters: teach Conquest (Part 1) before Control (Part 2) before Society (Part 3) — students need the military narrative pinned down before they can interpret the Domesday landholding pattern or the Church reforms.

Build the historic environment site in across multiple lessons, not just the final lesson. Reference Pevensey when teaching William's landing (Part 1), when teaching castles and patronage (Parts 1-2), and when teaching William II's reign (Part 1). The dedicated site lesson then synthesises rather than introduces.

Use Domesday extracts as a recurring source — short Latin entries with translations work well for 'describe two features' practice and source utility skills, even though source utility is technically a Paper 1 / Paper 2 Section A skill.

Comparative Anglo-Saxon vs Norman framing is required by the spec. Each major topic (government, society, Church, monasticism) needs a 'what was it like before' beat so students can answer 'how far did the Normans change X' questions.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edward the Confessor
key_individuals_and_groups.role: King of England 1042-1066. His childless death triggered the succession crisis. Likely promised the throne to William in 1051 (Norman claim) but on his deathbed gestured to Harold (English claim).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harold Godwinson
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Earl of Wessex, then King of England Jan-Oct 1066. Crowned the day after Edward's death. Defeated Hardrada at Stamford Bridge (25 Sep) but was killed at Hastings (14 Oct).

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Harald Hardrada
key_individuals_and_groups.role: King of Norway and rival claimant. Invaded the north of England in September 1066 with Tostig Godwinson. Killed at Stamford Bridge.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William the Conqueror (William I)
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Duke of Normandy. Claimed the English throne by promise and oath. Won at Hastings, crowned 25 Dec 1066. Reigned to 1087, dying in Normandy from a riding accident at Mantes.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: William II 'Rufus'
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's second son, King of England 1087-1100. Faced the 1088 rebellion (with Pevensey at its centre) when Norman barons backed his elder brother Robert Curthose. Killed in the New Forest in a hunting accident, 1100.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert Curthose
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's eldest son. Inherited Normandy in 1087 (not England) and led the 1088 rebellion against William Rufus.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Robert of Mortain
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's half-brother. Granted Pevensey Castle and vast lands across England. Backed the 1088 rebellion.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Odo of Bayeux
key_individuals_and_groups.role: William I's other half-brother. Bishop of Bayeux, Earl of Kent. Commissioned the Bayeux Tapestry. Imprisoned 1082; rebelled 1088.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Hereward 'the Wake'
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lincolnshire thegn who led English resistance from the Isle of Ely, 1070-71. Symbol of Anglo-Saxon defiance; later legend exaggerates his story.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Edgar Atheling
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Anglo-Saxon claimant — grandson of Edmund Ironside. Briefly elected king by the Witan after Hastings before submitting. Centre of multiple revolts.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Lanfranc of Bec
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Italian-born monk, prior at Bec in Normandy. Made Archbishop of Canterbury 1070 by William I. Drove the Norman Church reform — replaced Anglo-Saxon bishops, rebuilt cathedrals, asserted Canterbury primacy over York.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Anselm
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Lanfranc's successor at Bec and at Canterbury (from 1093). Clashed with William II over Church-state authority — early phase of the Investiture Controversy in England.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Stigand
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The Anglo-Saxon Archbishop of Canterbury whom William and the papacy considered illegitimate. Deposed in 1070 to make way for Lanfranc.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Alexander II
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Blessed William's invasion in 1066, sending a papal banner. The Church's pre-conquest endorsement framed the conquest as righteous reform.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Pope Gregory VII
key_individuals_and_groups.role: Drove the wider Investiture Controversy. William I refused to do homage to him for England, setting the pattern for Norman Church-state relations.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Tenants-in-chief
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The c.180 Norman lords who held land directly from the king (per Domesday). Backbone of the feudal pyramid.

key_individuals_and_groups.name: Anglo-Saxon thegns
key_individuals_and_groups.role: The displaced English landholding class. By 1086 fewer than 10% of pre-conquest landholders still held land — most had been killed, exiled or reduced to tenants of Norman lords.

lessons.title: Edward's Death and the Succession Crisis of 1066
lessons.description: Childless king, four claimants, and a kingdom on the edge — why January 1066 set everything in motion.
lessons.teaching_focus: Trace Edward the Confessor's reign and his ambiguous succession promises (William 1051, Harold's deathbed gesture, Hardrada's claim via Cnut). Explain why each of the four claimants — Harold, William, Hardrada, Edgar Atheling — believed they had the better case, and why the Witan went for Harold.
key_content: Edward the Confessor's reign and childlessness
1051 promise to William
Harold Godwinson's coronation 6 January 1066
Harald Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson
Edgar Atheling and the Witan's choice
Why the throne mattered: wealth and prestige of England in 1066
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Harold was a usurper. From the Anglo-Saxon perspective the Witan's choice was legitimate; the Norman framing of Harold-as-oathbreaker is post-1066 propaganda.

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings: the Battles of 1066
lessons.description: Two battles in three weeks: how the Vikings, the English and the Normans collided in autumn 1066.
lessons.teaching_focus: Run through Hardrada's invasion at Fulford and the English victory at Stamford Bridge (25 Sep), then the rapid march south, William's landing at Pevensey (28 Sep), and the Battle of Hastings (14 Oct). Stress Anglo-Saxon and Norman tactics — shield wall vs cavalry/archers — and the close-run nature of Hastings.
key_content: Battle of Fulford and Stamford Bridge
Anglo-Saxon shield wall and housecarls
William's landing at Pevensey
Hastings: terrain, feigned retreats, Harold's death
Why the battle was close-run, not inevitable
Tactics and military innovations: cavalry, archers, castles
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman cavalry made victory inevitable. The shield wall held until late afternoon; Harold's death (probably an arrow + a knight, not an arrow alone) and the resulting collapse decided it.

lessons.title: From Hastings to Coronation: William Takes the Throne
lessons.description: How William turned a battlefield win into a crown — and what Christmas Day 1066 actually looked like.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the post-Hastings march via Dover, Canterbury, Wallingford and Berkhamsted; the submission of Edgar Atheling and the Witan; the coronation at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066 and the riot outside; William's early conciliation policies (confirming Anglo-Saxon law, keeping some English officials).
key_content: Post-Hastings march and submissions
Berkhamsted: surrender of Edgar Atheling
Coronation at Westminster Abbey, 25 Dec 1066
Crowd panic and houses burned outside the abbey
Early conciliation of English nobility
William's first castles in London (the Tower) and elsewhere
lessons.misconception_to_target: That coronation = total control. William ruled only the south-east in early 1067; the Midlands, North and Welsh borderlands were still effectively independent.

lessons.title: Resistance and Revolt, 1067-1071
lessons.description: Kent, the South-West, the North, the Fens — five years of revolts that nearly unmade the conquest.
lessons.teaching_focus: Walk through the revolts: Kent and Eustace of Boulogne (1067), Exeter (1068), Edwin and Morcar in the North (1068), the Danish-backed northern revolt and the harrying of York (1069), Hereward at Ely (1070-71). Show how each revolt prompted more castles and harsher reprisals.
key_content: Eustace of Boulogne and Kent, 1067
Exeter siege, 1068
Earls Edwin and Morcar in the North
Danish fleet and the sack of York 1069
Hereward the Wake at Ely 1070-71
Castle-building as a response to revolt
lessons.misconception_to_target: That resistance was uncoordinated and doomed. Several revolts came close to forcing William out — the 1069 northern revolt with Danish fleet support was the most dangerous moment of his reign.

lessons.title: The Harrying of the North, 1069-1070
lessons.description: William's scorched-earth answer to rebellion — and a debate historians still cannot settle.
lessons.teaching_focus: Detail the winter campaign of 1069-70: villages razed, livestock killed, food stores destroyed across Yorkshire and beyond. Use Orderic Vitalis's '100,000 dead' alongside Domesday's 'waste' entries to teach historiographical caution. Stress the political effect: the North was not seriously rebellious again under William I.
key_content: The 1069 northern revolt and Danish fleet
William's winter campaign
Scale and methods of destruction
Orderic Vitalis and John of Worcester accounts
Domesday 'waste' entries
Modern historiographical debate (Hugh Thomas vs older readings)
Long-term effect on northern landholding
lessons.misconception_to_target: That '100,000 dead' is a fact. It is a chronicle figure written decades later by a writer who hated cruelty. Modern historians treat it as evidence of perceived horror, not a head-count.

lessons.title: Feudalism and the Norman Land Settlement
lessons.description: Land for service, lord and vassal, knights' fees: how William rebuilt English society as a pyramid.
lessons.teaching_focus: Explain the feudal pyramid (king > tenants-in-chief > sub-tenants > peasants) using concrete cases: Robert of Mortain holding Pevensey of the king, sub-infeudating manors to his own knights. Cover military service obligations, knights' fees, patronage, and the dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy. Flag the historiographical debate (Reynolds) — students learn the working model, but understand it's a model.
key_content: The feudal pyramid: king, tenants-in-chief, sub-tenants, peasants
Knights' fees and military service obligation
Sub-infeudation and patronage
Dispossession of Anglo-Saxon thegns by 1086
Robert of Mortain as a case study
Reynolds critique: 'feudalism' as a model not a system
lessons.misconception_to_target: That William invented feudalism. Norman France already had this pattern; William transplanted and intensified it. And — per Reynolds — calling it 'a system' overstates its tidiness.

lessons.title: Castles: Instruments of Conquest and Control
lessons.description: How c.500 motte-and-bailey castles and a few stone keeps held down a kingdom of two million.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the spread of castles from c.50 in 1066 to c.500 by 1100. Distinguish motte-and-bailey (timber, fast to build) from stone keeps (Tower of London's White Tower, Colchester). Stress castles as instruments of conquest first — projection of lordly power, garrisoning towns, controlling river crossings — and only secondarily defensive. Foreshadow Pevensey as the unit's specified site.
key_content: Castles before 1066 (rare in Anglo-Saxon England)
Motte-and-bailey design and rapid construction
Tower of London and the White Tower
Castle siting: river crossings, town centres, road junctions
Castles as projection of power, not just defence
Sample sites: Berkhamsted, York, Lincoln, Pevensey
lessons.misconception_to_target: That castles were only defensive. They were political tools — visible threats to local populations and bases for armed retinues to project power outward.

lessons.title: Norman Government, Justice and the Anglo-Saxon Inheritance
lessons.description: Sheriffs, hundred courts, ordeals and 'murdrum': what the Normans kept and what they bolted on.
lessons.teaching_focus: Show what the Normans inherited (shires, hundreds, sheriffs, the writ, Anglo-Saxon law codes) and what they added (forest law, the murdrum fine, French as the language of the elite courts, expanded royal justice via itinerant officials). Compare Anglo-Saxon and Norman aristocracies and their different cultures of authority.
key_content: Inherited Anglo-Saxon government: shires, hundreds, sheriffs, writs
Anglo-Saxon and Norman aristocracies compared
Norman additions: forest law, murdrum fine
Justice and the legal system: ordeals, trial by combat
Inheritance law (primogeniture vs partible)
Continuity beneath rupture (Hugh Thomas thesis)
lessons.question_type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman government was a clean break. The framework — shires, sheriffs, hundred courts — was inherited largely intact; the personnel changed.

lessons.title: The Domesday Book, 1086
lessons.description: A whole kingdom audited in two years: what William really wanted to know — and what we get to read 940 years later.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the 1085 Christmas council at Gloucester, the survey commissioners and procedures, the Great Domesday and Little Domesday volumes, and the speed of the operation. Dig into purposes: tax assessment (geld capacity), recording the new tenurial structure post-conquest, settling disputes between tenants-in-chief. Use real entries to model 'describe two features' practice.
key_content: 1085 Christmas council and the decision to survey
Commissioners, juries and procedure
Great and Little Domesday
Purpose: tax, tenurial record, dispute settlement
What Domesday reveals about post-conquest landholding (c.180 tenants-in-chief; <10% Anglo-Saxon survival)
Why historians treat 'waste' entries cautiously
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Domesday was a legal land registry. It was primarily fiscal and political — an audit of who held what and how much it could be taxed.

lessons.title: Daily Life: Towns, Villages and Economic Change
lessons.description: For most people the king never visited — but the new lord did. Life on the manor under Norman rule.
lessons.teaching_focus: Compare Anglo-Saxon and Norman rural and urban life: villages, manorial farming, seasonal labour, markets, towns. Cover the impact of forest law (royal hunting reserves, savage penalties), urban changes (French quarters in major towns, new market grants), economic continuity for most peasants, and the way Norman lords reshaped landscapes (parks, castles, burhs).
key_content: Anglo-Saxon village and manorial life
Towns and markets before and after 1066
French quarters in conquered towns (e.g. Norwich, Nottingham)
Forest law and royal hunting reserves
Seasonal labour and food
Continuity for most peasants beneath the Norman elite
lessons.question_type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
lessons.misconception_to_target: That Norman conquest revolutionised peasant life immediately. For most ordinary people, daily life and labour patterns continued; the lord's name and language changed at the top.

lessons.title: Lanfranc and the Reform of the English Church
lessons.description: An Italian monk, an English Church and a programme of cathedrals, councils and Norman bishops.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover the Anglo-Saxon Church before 1066 (Stigand's pluralism, monastic centres at Worcester and Canterbury). Trace Lanfranc's appointment in 1070, his replacement of Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans, the 1075 Council of London reorganising dioceses, the great cathedral building programme (Canterbury, Durham, St Albans, Old Sarum), and the Canterbury-vs-York primacy dispute.
key_content: Anglo-Saxon Church before 1066: structure, learning, criticisms
Stigand and his deposition 1070
Lanfranc's appointment and reform programme
Replacement of Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans
1075 Council of London: dioceses moved to towns
Cathedral building: Canterbury, Durham, St Albans
Canterbury-York primacy dispute
lessons.misconception_to_target: That the Anglo-Saxon Church was decadent and Lanfranc cleaned it up. The pre-conquest Church had reform impulses; Lanfranc's main effect was Norman political control of personnel and a building programme that visibly stamped Norman authority.

lessons.title: Monasticism, Learning and the Investiture Controversy
lessons.description: New abbeys, new schools, Latin and the vernacular — and the row over who owns the bishops.
lessons.teaching_focus: Cover Norman monasticism: new abbeys (Battle Abbey on the Hastings field, Selby, Tewkesbury), Cluniac and Benedictine reform, monastic schools, Latin learning. Then turn to Church-state tensions: William I's relationship with the papacy (refused homage to Gregory VII), William II's exploitation of vacant Church lands, Anselm's clash with Rufus from 1093 — the English phase of the Investiture Controversy.
key_content: Norman abbey-building: Battle, Selby, Tewkesbury
Monastic life and reform
Schools, Latin and the vernacular
William I and Pope Gregory VII
Church wealth and royal exploitation under William II
Anselm's clash with William Rufus
Beginnings of the Investiture Controversy in England
lessons.misconception_to_target: That the Investiture Controversy was a continental problem only. England was drawn in from the 1090s through Anselm's struggle with Rufus over Church appointments and obedience to Rome.

lesson_count_check.note: Spec calls for roughly 3+4+3+3 across the four parts. We have weighted Parts 1 and 2 slightly heavier (5+5+2+1) because (a) the conquest narrative anchors everything, (b) Part 2 contains the Domesday and feudalism content that drives many essay questions, and (c) Pevensey runs as a thread through Lessons 2, 6, 7 and 12 before being formally synthesised in Lesson 13. Two Church lessons (Lanfranc; monasticism+investiture) cover all spec bullets without forcing thin coverage.

spec_bullet_coverage.part_1_establishing_control_harrying_rev: Lessons 3, 4, 5 (and revisited in Lesson 13 for the 1088 siege)

gaps: Lesson 7 (Castles) introduces the White Tower in passing. If AQA later confirms a different 2026 site (highly unlikely — the 2026-2028 cycle is publicly announced), the Pevensey-specific synthesis in Lesson 13 would need a rebuild.
Numismatic and seal evidence for Norman government is not covered explicitly — relegated to a sidebar in Lesson 8 if assets allow. AQA examiners do not usually require it.

Bayeux Tapestry is referenced (Odo of Bayeux, Lesson 4) but not given a dedicated lesson. Decision: it's evidence not subject matter, so it threads through Lessons 1-3 as visual material rather than its own slot.

site_2026.location: East Sussex, on the south coast of England
site_2026.source: aqa.org.uk/news/gcse-history-historic-environment-sites-2026-2028 (sites announced for 2026-2028 cycle: 2026 Pevensey Castle, 2027 The Battle of Hastings, 2028 The White Tower)
site_2026.why_relevant: Pevensey was William's landing site on 28 September 1066, where he sheltered his fleet of c.700 ships inside a Roman fort and built his first English fortification — directly anchoring the conquest narrative to a specific physical place. The castle was then granted to Robert of Mortain (William's half-brother), who turned it into a permanent stone castle and used the Roman walls as his outer bailey. In 1088 it was the focus of a six-week siege by William II (Rufus) when Robert backed Robert Curthose's rebellion — making the site relevant across all three reigns of the spec (William I, William II) and across all four parts of the depth study: conquest (Part 1), castles and feudal landholding (Parts 1 & 2), Church links via St Nicolas's Church inside the bailey (Part 3), and the historic environment essay itself (Part 4).
key_features_for_essays: Roman fort (Anderida, c.AD 290) reused as the outer wall — illustrates Norman opportunism in repurposing existing fortifications
Coastal peninsula location controlling Channel crossing — strategic for communication with Normandy
Inner bailey ditch and stone keep added under Robert of Mortain — shows transition from temporary timber fortification to permanent Norman stronghold
1088 siege by William Rufus — links the site to William II's struggle to secure his inheritance against his brother Robert Curthose
Connections to the wider conquest: William's first foothold, granted as patronage to a tenant-in-chief, garrisoned during revolts

historic_environment_dropped_for_v1.reason: L13 anchored on Pevensey Castle (rotating 2026 site)

content_agent_guardrails_for_he: Do NOT reference the AQA-specified 2026 historic environment site for this option (e.g. Globe, Pevensey, Caernarfon, Ham House). The site rotates yearly and we are deferring that content. Period-general castle/theatre/site content is fine where naturally part of the topic.
